source: Chang, Chen, Mellers & Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment (Table 4, re-opened in full text)
finding: Trained forecasters beat controls in all four tournament years, with random assignment at entry. Gain was 10% (Y1), 12% (Y2), 6% (Y3), 7% (Y4).
limits: In Y4 the running text swaps the n and mean labels versus Table 4; Table 4 has trained as better. Y1 prob-trained mean misprinted in text. Volunteers, not a random sample. Brier z-scored within question.
agent_relevance: Confirms the human numbers behind K01 and K03. The effect is real in-sample but shrinks from 12% to 6-7%.

source: Chang et al. (2016) mediation analysis by year (section 3.5, Figures 2-5)
finding: Gap 6 closed. The text reports the indirect effect through forecasts per question as significant in Y1 and Y3 only. Y2 and Y4 are not significant. Agent a was right about Y4, agent b was right about Y2; both years fail. The paper's own summary line says three of the four years, which does not match its Results text.
numbers: Y1: indirect effect -0.02, 95% CI -0.04 to -0.01, p=.01 (10,000 bootstrap draws). Y2: training to forecasts-per-question coefficient not significant, bootstrapped indirect effect not significant (n=399). Y3: training to forecasts/question p=0.06, forecasts/question to accuracy p=0.001, indirect -0.02, CI -0.04 to -0.01, p=0.05 (n=213). Y4: neither path significant (p=0.20), indirect effect not significant (n=221).
quote: The indirect effect was not significant (Figure 5).
limits: Y3 is borderline (p=0.05). Mediator is forecasts per question, a behaviour measure. Mediation here is cross-sectional.
agent_relevance: Weakens K05: practice-mediation holds in 2 of 4 years by the Results text, not 3 of 4. Do not claim forced update rounds explain the training gain.

source: Chang et al. (2016) Table 9 and section 2.1: veterans who stayed in the same condition
finding: Partial answer to gap 4. People who returned in later years were kept in their original condition. Trained veterans still beat control veterans in later years, so the effect persisted in the same people for at least one more year. Prior experience alone gave no significant gain.
numbers: Y2 veterans (n=148 control, 153 trained): raw Brier 0.39 vs 0.34, std +0.05 vs -0.11. Y2 new forecasters (n=46 vs 52): std +0.03 vs -0.07, 13%, p<.001. Y3 veterans (n=56 vs 53): 0.36 vs 0.33, std +0.05 vs -0.08, about 9%. Y3 new (n=60 vs 44): 0.33 vs 0.32, std -0.05 vs -0.10, 3%.
limits: Only people who met participation thresholds and opted back in are veterans (attrition selection). The paper does not say whether returning trained people redid the module; Y3 onward had a revised module. No delayed retest without new feedback. Veterans had a year of practice with Brier feedback.
agent_relevance: Persistence into a second year is supported in the same people, but it is confounded with ongoing feedback and practice. Nothing here says a one-shot instruction persists without feedback.

source: Chang et al. (2016) Tables 8 and 10: forecasting volume by condition
finding: Trained people did not make more forecasts overall. They made more forecasts per question they chose, which fits a concentrate-on-fewer-questions story.
numbers: Forecasts per subject (no training / training): Y1 86.76 / 84.29 (scenario 73.15); Y2 139.03 / 127.81; Y3 118.21 / 113.09; Y4 149.02 / 141.84. Forecasts per question per user (no training / training): Y1 1.35 / 1.58; Y2 1.47 / 1.56; Y3 1.90 / 4.27; Y4 2.53 / 3.11.
limits: Column order of Table 8 read from table text by me. Observational. The Y3 gap (4.27 vs 1.90) is large but Y3 mediation was only borderline.
agent_relevance: Updating more on fewer items is a mechanism candidate. It supports a state that re-forecasts the same item, but the mediation test is weak (d02).

source: Chang et al. (2016) Tables 5-7: which CHAMPS KNOW principles went with better forecasts (Y4 only)
finding: Only comparison classes (C) went with clearly better forecasts. Post-mortem (P) and other perspectives (O) went with worse ones. 69% of explanations were self-classified. Probabilistic principles beat political ones overall.
numbers: Std Brier, comparison classes n=580 mean 0.17; hunt for information n=2,992 mean 0.38. ANOVA: C MS 39.34, F=12.28, p<.001; P F=9.38, p=.002; hunt F=2.83, p=.092; adjust/update F=0.00, p=.948; math models F=2.35, p=.125. Political: other perspectives F=10.92, p<.001; norms F=2.82, p=.093. CHAMPS as a group F=11.96, p<.001; KNOW group F=0.08, p=.783.
limits: Correlational. Forecasts scored per explanation assuming independence though one person wrote many. Principle choice is self-selected after the forecast. Trained arm only.
agent_relevance: Supports K04: if one reference-class step is tested in the agent, it is the strongest single candidate. The adjust-and-update principle shows no signal.

source: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang & Tenney (2017) Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition, Management Science (Table 1, re-opened)
finding: Gap 7 closed. The source Table 1 matches the earlier figures: training lowered overconfidence from 4.3 to 2.0 points for individuals and 2.8 to 0.7 for teams, mostly by lowering confidence, not by raising the hit rate.
numbers: N=2,860 forecasters, 344 IARPA questions, three tournament years (about 9 months each). Confidence / hit rate / overconfidence (SD): autonomous no training 64.9 (8.5) / 60.7 (10.3) / 4.3a (9.4); autonomous training 63.5 (8.2) / 61.5 (10.6) / 2.0b (9.7); team no training 65.8 (7.9) / 62.9 (12.7) / 2.8a,b (12.5); team training 64.3 (8.4) / 63.6 (11.0) / 0.7b (7.3). Different letters differ at Bonferroni-adjusted 95% CIs. Training did not interact with time.
quote: Training appeared to reduce overconfidence similarly over the entire forecasting year
limits: The test is a Bonferroni CI grouping, not an effect size. Team-no-training (2.8a,b) does not differ from either solo cell. Scenario-training and other arms are dropped. Hit-rate gain from training is 0.8 points solo and 0.7 in teams. Training was one hour online before any forecast.
agent_relevance: A calibration guardrail mostly acts as a confidence cut. For an LLM check Brier and ECE, and report hit rate separately, so a confidence cut is not mistaken for skill.

source: Moore et al. (2017) description of earlier lab training and its own durability claim
finding: Gap 8, partly. The source describes Lichtenstein & Fischhoff 1980 and Stone & Opel 2000 as long, costly programmes whose benefit degraded and did not carry far from the training context. It adds that its own year-long durability may owe to continuous outcome feedback.
numbers: Lichtenstein & Fischhoff 1980: 45 minutes of calibration training plus 22 hour-long testing sessions. Stone & Opel 2000: 6 sessions of 2 hours each. Moore: forecasters kept receiving Brier feedback on a leaderboard.
quote: with degradation over time and limited generalization beyond the training context
limits: Still second-hand: I could not open the 1980 or 2000 papers. No effect sizes or decay rates from those two were recovered. Only session counts and the qualitative verdict come from Moore.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open on exact numbers. The qualitative verdict stands: gains need ongoing feedback. An agent with no feedback loop should not expect durable training.

source: Kelly & Mandel (2024) The effect of calibration training on the calibration of intelligence analysts' judgments, Applied Cognitive Psychology (OSF preprint, full text)
finding: Closest independent test (gap 1): a different group, a commercial 3-4 hour calibration course, 70 intelligence analysts, pre/post design with no control group. Training cut overconfidence on interval estimates but pushed binary judgments toward underconfidence, and the two changes were uncorrelated.
numbers: Miscalibration before M=.33, after M=.18; F(1,69)=59.48. Interval task: miscalibration down, t(69)=8.80, d=1.05; bias down, t(69)=9.83, d=1.17. Binary task: miscalibration not significantly changed (slightly worse, t(69)=1.80, p=.076, d=0.22); bias up toward underconfidence, t(69)=3.11, p=.003, d=0.37. Cross-task correlation of change: miscalibration r(68)=-.06, p=.638; bias r(68)=-.10, p=.411. Post-test about 2.2 days after training.
limits: Not the Chang/Tetlock probability module: a different course (equivalent bet test, pre-mortem, calibration tests). Pre/post only, no control, short delay, almanac-style items, not real forecasts. Training shifted bias, not discrimination.
agent_relevance: Warns that calibration training can be a blanket confidence shift. For the agent, measure shrink in both directions and per task type.

source: Stone, Luu, Costello & Somerville (2023) Automated calibration training for forecasters, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making (Crossref abstract)
finding: Independent of Tetlock (Stone co-wrote the 2000 calibration paper). Two experiments (baseball game outcomes; a modified blackjack bust task): individualized feedback lowered confidence in initially overconfident forecasters, and gave better overall calibration in Experiment 2 only.
numbers: Abstract only. No sample sizes or effect sizes recovered (publisher page returned 403).
limits: Abstract only. Lab tasks, no year-long follow-up. Feedback is the training here, not a probability lesson.
agent_relevance: Supports the point that feedback on one's own calibration moves confidence. A fixed instruction without feedback is a weaker analogue.

source: Schoenegger, Greenberg, Grishin, Marshall & Karger (2025) Prompt engineering LLMs' forecasting capabilities, Study 1: reference-class prompts (re-read, both tables)
finding: Gap 2, partly. Prompts that tell the model to start from base rates or reference classes lowered Brier by about 0.004 to 0.019, not reliably. The explicit anti-overconfidence prompt did nothing. Reference-class effects are significant only in the simple t-tests, not in the preregistered mixed model.
numbers: Four models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 3.1 405B), 100 ForecastBench questions, temperature 0, 2,000 max output tokens, 38 prompts. Control Brier: GPT-4o 0.215, Haiku 0.214, Llama 0.227, Sonnet 0.208. Mixed model (diff vs control, adj p): Frequency-Based -0.014 (.774); Base Rate First -0.011 (.774); Multiple Reference Classes -0.004 (p=.565, adj .774); Analogical -0.002; Anti-biasing (overconfidence) 0.000. One-sample t-tests (mean diff, adj p): Frequency-Based -0.019 (.022); Base Rate First -0.016 (.036); Step-Back -0.015 (.036); Multiple Reference Classes -0.009 (.233); Anti-biasing overconfidence -0.004 (.362); N about 390 per prompt.
limits: No equal-token control: output length was capped, not matched. N is question x model rows, not independent. Multiple Reference Classes, the closest match to the human C step, was weaker than Base Rate First.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that a lone reference-class step helps an LLM at equal tokens. Test in our harness with matched tokens and repeated runs.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Study 1: distance from 50% and the harmful Bayesian prompts (Tables 3, 4, 5)
finding: Gap 3, partly. The two harmful prompts were also the two that moved forecasts furthest from 50%. The paper offers one explanation (propose-and-evaluate confusion) but never tests a shrink or calibration step, so reversal is untested.
numbers: Mean absolute distance from 0.5: Bayesian Reasoning 0.199, Propose-Evaluate-Select 0.175, Chain of Thought 0.172, Control 0.134, Anti-biasing (anchoring) 0.119. Mixed model vs control: Bayesian +0.030 (z 5.44, p<.001), Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.033 (z 6.12, p<.001); the other 36 prompts not significant. t-test table: Bayesian +0.025 (adj p .036), P-E-S +0.028 (adj p .010). Mean forecast: Bayesian 0.476 (SD 0.250) vs control 0.453 (SD 0.185).
limits: Correlational across prompts: CoT is also more extreme (0.172) yet scored -0.011, so extremity alone does not explain the harm. No post-hoc rescaling experiment in the paper.
agent_relevance: Do not add an explicit Bayes-update step (SCHEMA 4b). If any numeric update step is added, test it with and without a shrink-to-50 or shrink-to-base-rate post-step.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Study 2: composite prompts and reasoning models (Table 8)
finding: Gap 5, partly. With o1 and o1-mini included, no prompt improved accuracy in the preregistered model, including the combined Base Rate First + Frequency-Based prompt. Effects were largely identical across models. The superforecaster-written Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt was significantly worse.
numbers: Brier: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 405B 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.207. Mixed model estimates: All Human -0.009, Frequency+CoT -0.008, CoT+Deep Breath -0.006, All -0.006, Base Rate First+Frequency -0.004; all adj p about .985. Forecasts returned: o1-mini 1,674; GPT-4o and Llama 1,893 each (refusals). Mean forecast: o1 41.5%; Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt 50.0%; Base Rate+Frequency 38.4%.
limits: Prompt only, no retrieval, so this answers frozen-retrieval only for o1-class models of 2024. Newer 2025-2026 reasoning models were not covered. o1 itself scored worse than GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Training-style prompts are not shown to help a reasoning model. Treat any scaffold gain as unproven until measured on the target model.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies? (arXiv 2406.04446, text re-read)
finding: A base-rate pipeline made an LLM forecaster worse than a one-line prompt. The authors trace it to a bias: the plain prompt predicts low probabilities, which pays off because most events resolve No.
numbers: 351 validation events. Brier: human prediction market 0.1334; basic baseline 0.1221; Forecaster prompt 0.1483; breakdown 0.1895; base rates 0.1562; both sides 0.1553; crowd of personas 0.1706; news API 0.1235. Weighted Brier (Yes and No events equal): human 0.1746, basic 0.1955, base rates 0.2540, crowd 0.1860. Average probability: human 0.3280, basic 0.2529, one minus reversed event 0.3965; Brier of reversed version 0.1814.
limits: Model name not extracted in my read. Rationale-first prompts raise probabilities, so results depend on the share of Yes outcomes in the set. Single dataset of market events.
agent_relevance: Prompt steps change the overall level of probabilities. Any scaffold gain must be checked against a constant-base-rate forecast and a symmetric (reversed) test.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting (re-read: scratchpad content and ablations)
finding: Gap 9, partly. The tuned scratchpad prompt already contained a step to check over- or underconfidence and consider historical base rates, yet with no retrieval and no fine-tuning the system scored 0.206, about equal to the best plain baseline 0.208. Retrieval and fine-tuning carried the gain. Fine-tuning taught the model which reasoning to use without the instructions.
numbers: Ablation Brier (crowd 0.146): full system 0.179; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 with base GPT-4 0.182; base GPT-4, no fine-tune 0.186 (+0.007); no fine-tune and no retrieval 0.206. Zero-shot vs scratchpad test Brier, GPT-4-1106 0.208 vs 0.209; GPT-4-0613 0.219 vs 0.222; Claude-2.1 0.220 vs 0.215; Llama-2-7B 0.353 vs 0.264. Fine-tuning: 13,253 of 73,632 self-generated reasonings kept (beat the crowd), trained on the 6,000 most recent for 2 epochs.
limits: Retrieval and fine-tuning share credit; the fine-tuning gain (0.007) is small compared with retrieval (about 0.020). Brier on this set is not comparable with other sets.
agent_relevance: About 0.02 Brier came from retrieval, 0.007 from fine-tuning, about 0 from reasoning-prompt content. Only the fine-tuning part could in principle become few-shot memory.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen & van Steenkiste (2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2503.17523; full text)
finding: Gap 10, partly. Fine-tuning small models on worked examples from a Bayesian assistant, including its early wrong guesses, beat fine-tuning on always-correct oracle answers and generalized to new domains. Prompting alone (chain of thought, non-interactive context) did not improve accuracy. Not about forecasting, and it is fine-tuning, not in-context teaching.
numbers: Flight recommendation task, 5 rounds. Bayesian Assistant final-round accuracy 81%; human participants 58%. Original LLMs plateaued after round 1 (Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B roughly 36-50%). Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time and beat oracle-tuned models on all three base models (p<0.001). Generalizes to hotels and web shopping. CoT prompt performed similarly to baseline.
limits: Per-model tuned accuracies not extracted (figure values garbled in text). Only supervised fine-tuning was tested; no comparison of worked examples in context vs abstract instructions. Task is preference inference, not event forecasting.
agent_relevance: No evidence that worked examples beat abstract instructions for forecasting. The signal is that teaching by showing uncertain intermediate guesses helped. In a scaffold this could become a few-shot trace, untested.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based reinforcement learning to predict the future (headline numbers as confirmed in critique.md; not re-read this session)
finding: For gap 9: RL on resolved questions moved a 14B model by 0.025 Brier. Compared with Schoenegger's best prompt (-0.011 to -0.019, other set) and Halawi's fine-tune (0.007), RL is the larger lever, but it is not a scaffold step.
numbers: From critique: 1,265 questions; ReMax ensemble 0.190 [0.178, 0.203], ECE 0.062; Modified-GRPO 0.192 / 0.054; o1 0.202 / 0.093; base model 0.215.
limits: Not re-opened by me. Cross-paper Brier comparison is invalid (different question sets). Nobody has run equal-token scaffold versus RL.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: no study moves RL gains into fixed scaffold steps.

source: Karimi Motahhar & Gruca (2025) How does training improve individual forecasts? Compensatory and non-compensatory biases in geopolitical forecasts, IJF
finding: Found by Crossref search: an outside group analysing geopolitical forecast data with a bias model. Abstract and text not reachable (closed access).
limits: Not opened. Probably a reanalysis of GJP data, so not an independent replication even if it agrees.
agent_relevance: Worth reading next for a mechanism account of which biases training removes.

source: Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer (2001) Teaching Bayesian reasoning in less than two hours; Benson & Onkal (1992) feedback and training of probability forecasters (located, not opened)
finding: Two independent human-training studies were located by Crossref. Full text was blocked (bot check on the MPG repository; SSRN redirect). I did not bypass the blocks.
limits: Unopened. Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer teach natural-frequency Bayesian problems, not event forecasting.
agent_relevance: Targets for a later pass on gap 1.
